title: Membranes: The Impermeable Sheet That Builds Itself

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: A sodium ion (radius about 1.0 Å) is smaller than a water molecule (about 1.4 Å). Why does water still cross a bare lipid bilayer about ten billion times faster?
cards.back: The membrane is not a sieve. Na⁺'s full charge holds a tight water shell, and entering the oily core means giving up that shell, a huge energy toll. Charge, not size, decides.
cards.quote: A sodium ion is smaller than a water molecule, yet water crosses a bare lipid bilayer about ten billion times faster.

cards.front: A solute's {{c1::electrochemical gradient}} is the combined push it feels from a difference in concentration and, if it is charged, a difference in voltage across the membrane.
cards.quote: A solute's electrochemical gradient is the combined push it feels from two differences across the membrane

cards.front: Every crossing of a membrane answers two separate questions. What are they, and what sets each one?
cards.back: How fast: across a bare bilayer, the toll for leaving water; a protein speeds it with a cheaper polar path. Which way: for a solute moving on its own, only its electrochemical gradient.
cards.quote: For a solute moving on its own, that is set only by its electrochemical gradient.

cards.front: Phospholipids form a bilayer in water with no ATP and no covalent bonds. What drives the assembly, and where does the energy come from?
cards.back: The hydrophobic effect, which is entropic. Water caged around the oily tails is released into disorder when the tails cluster, so the entropy of the system rises. The energy comes from water.
cards.quote: When the tails huddle together, that caged water is released into disorder, and the entropy of the system rises.

cards.front: A fine glass needle is pushed through a cell membrane and pulled out. A plastic bag gets the same treatment. Predict what happens to each hole.
cards.back: The membrane hole seals; the bag stays torn. Noncovalent forces hold the bilayer, so no bonds broke. Lipids at the edge now expose tails to water, and the hydrophobic effect pulls them closed.
cards.why: The bag is covalently bonded plastic. A living cell also speeds membrane repair by fusing vesicles at the wound.
cards.quote: No bonds broke when the needle went in, because none held the lipids together.

cards.front: The energy an ion must pay to give up its water shell and enter the oily core of a bilayer is the toll for leaving water, also called the {{c1::desolvation penalty}}.
cards.quote: The cost of that trade is the toll for leaving water, also called the desolvation penalty.

cards.front: Rank these by how easily they cross a bare lipid bilayer: glucose, CO₂, K⁺, urea. What single feature are you ranking by?
cards.back: CO₂, then urea, then glucose, then K⁺ far behind. The feature is how strongly each holds water: a nonpolar gas pays almost no toll, polar molecules a moderate one, a full charge the largest.
cards.why: Size matters a little; charge matters most. Glucose sits below urea in the lesson's permeability ordering.
cards.quote: Small gases such as O₂ and CO₂ sit at the top, at about 1 cm/s and above.

cards.front: Across the solutes a cell cares about, permeability coefficients through a bare bilayer span about how many orders of magnitude, and where does Na⁺ sit?
cards.back: About twelve orders of magnitude. Small gases are at about 1 cm/s and above; Na⁺ is at the bottom, near 10⁻¹² cm/s.
cards.quote: Across the solutes a cell cares about, it spans about twelve orders of magnitude.

cards.front: Roughly how large is the hydration energy of K⁺ and Na⁺, and how much larger is it for Na⁺?
cards.back: Roughly 300 to 400 kJ/mol (convention-dependent), with about 70 kJ/mol more for the smaller Na⁺, whose charge is packed more tightly. A hydrogen bond is about 20 kJ/mol.
cards.quote: roughly 300 to 400 kJ/mol for K⁺ and Na⁺, with about 70 kJ/mol more for the smaller Na⁺

cards.front: Indole is tryptophan's aromatic ring alone; tryptophan adds an amino and a carboxyl group, both charged at pH 7. Indole crosses a bilayer many orders of magnitude faster. What does this pair show?
cards.back: Charge, not size, sets permeability. The ring is the same and the weight differs by less than twofold, so only the charged groups, each paying the toll for leaving water, explain the gap.
cards.quote: The ring is the same and the weight differs by less than twofold, so neither size nor weight can explain the gap.

cards.front: What is a membrane's transition temperature, Tm?
cards.back: The midpoint of the change from an ordered, nearly frozen gel (below Tm) to a disordered, fluid sheet (above Tm).
cards.quote: Below a transition temperature, Tm, the tails pack into an ordered, nearly frozen gel.
cards.section: A separate question: keeping the sheet fluid

cards.front: How do fatty-acid chain length and a cis double bond each change a membrane's Tm, and why?
cards.back: Longer tails pack more snugly and raise Tm. A cis double bond puts a roughly 30-degree kink in the tail that prevents tight packing and lowers Tm.
cards.why: Trans double bonds leave the tail straight, so trans fats pack like saturated fats.
cards.quote: Longer fatty-acid tails pack more snugly and raise Tm.
cards.section: A separate question: keeping the sheet fluid

cards.front: A cell must keep its membrane fluid after a shift to a colder temperature. Should it make its lipid tails longer and more saturated, or shorter and more cis-unsaturated? Why?
cards.back: Shorter and more cis-unsaturated. Kinked, shorter tails pack less tightly and lower Tm, so the membrane stays above its transition temperature and fluid in the cold.
cards.why: Rests on the rules that length raises Tm and a cis double bond lowers it.
cards.quote: A cis double bond puts a roughly 30-degree kink in the tail that prevents tight packing and lowers Tm.
cards.section: A separate question: keeping the sheet fluid

cards.front: Cholesterol is called the membrane's thermostat. How does it act in the cold and in the warm?
cards.back: Cold: its rigid ring body jams between lipids so they cannot pack into a gel. Warm: its flat rings restrain the upper tails so the membrane is not too runny.
cards.why: It does not hold a set temperature; it broadens and flattens the gel-to-fluid change.
cards.quote: it broadens and flattens the gel-to-fluid change, so fluidity changes less as temperature changes
cards.section: A separate question: keeping the sheet fluid

cards.front: In FRAP on a labeled membrane protein, the bleached spot recovers quickly but plateaus at 50% of the original intensity. What do the rate and the plateau each report, and what do you conclude?
cards.back: The recovery rate gives the diffusion coefficient; the completeness gives the mobile fraction. Here the mobile molecules diffuse fast, but half the labeled protein cannot move, often because it is anchored to the cytoskeleton.
cards.quote: How fast the spot recovers gives the diffusion coefficient. How completely it recovers gives the mobile fraction.

cards.front: Why is lateral diffusion of a lipid fast while flip-flop from one leaflet to the other is glacially slow?
cards.back: Lateral motion stays within one leaflet. To flip, the polar head would have to cross the oily core and pay the toll for leaving water.
cards.quote: To flip, the polar head would have to cross the oily core.

cards.front: Lipid flip-flop happens at a useful rate only with dedicated enzymes: {{c1::flippases}} move lipids to the inner leaflet, floppases to the outer, and scramblases either way.
cards.quote: flippases move lipids to the inner leaflet, floppases to the outer, and scramblases either way

cards.front: Why does phosphatidylserine (PS) stay on the inner leaflet of a resting cell, and what does its outward flip signal in a dying cell?
cards.back: Flip-flop is slow on its own, and ATP-driven flippases keep returning PS to the inner leaflet. When a cell dies, PS flips outward and becomes an "eat me" signal for the immune system.
cards.why: Rests on two rules: asymmetry is kept by ATP-driven flippases working against slow flip-flop, and outward PS is the signal seen when a cell dies.
cards.quote: When a cell dies, phosphatidylserine flips outward, and that becomes an "eat me" signal for the immune system.

cards.front: What operational test distinguishes a peripheral from an integral membrane protein?
cards.back: Peripheral proteins come off with high salt or a pH change. Integral proteins release only when detergent dissolves the membrane around them.
cards.quote: Peripheral proteins come off with high salt or a pH change.

cards.front: Why is an alpha-helix a good way for a protein to cross the oily core of a bilayer?
cards.back: Its backbone N–H and C=O groups hydrogen-bond to each other along the helix, so the backbone pays its own toll, and its hydrophobic side chains face the oil.
cards.quote: its backbone groups hydrogen-bond to each other along the helix, so the backbone pays its own toll

cards.front: An alpha-helix rises 1.5 Å per residue. About how many hydrophobic residues does it take to span a 3 nm oily core once?
cards.back: 3 nm = 30 Å. 30 Å ÷ 1.5 Å per residue = 20 residues.
cards.quote: A helix rises 1.5 Å per residue, so about 20 hydrophobic residues span the 3 nm oily core once

cards.front: In a typical neuron the inside of the membrane sits around {{c1::60 to 70 millivolts negative}} relative to outside.
cards.back: Most cells fall between about −35 and −80 mV; red blood cells are about −10 mV.
cards.quote: In a typical neuron the inside sits around 60 to 70 millivolts negative.

cards.front: K⁺ is 4 mM outside and 140 mM inside, Vm = −70 mV, 37 °C (RT = 2.58 kJ/mol, F = 96.5 kJ/mol·V). Find ΔG for moving 1 mol K⁺ into the cell. Which way does K⁺ tend to go?
cards.back: Concentration: 2.58 × ln(140/4) = +9.2 kJ/mol. Voltage: (+1) × 96.5 × (−0.070) = −6.8 kJ/mol. Total ≈ +2.4 kJ/mol. Moving in is uphill, so K⁺ tends to leave.
cards.quote: Moving potassium in is uphill, so on its own potassium tends to leave the cell.

cards.front: Na⁺ is 145 mM outside and 12 mM inside, Vm = −70 mV, 37 °C (RT = 2.58 kJ/mol, F = 96.5 kJ/mol·V). Find ΔG for moving 1 mol Na⁺ into the cell.
cards.back: Concentration: 2.58 × ln(12/145) = −6.4 kJ/mol. Voltage: (+1) × 96.5 × (−0.070) = −6.8 kJ/mol. Total ≈ −13.2 kJ/mol: both terms favor entry, well downhill.
cards.quote: Both parts are negative and about equal, so the move is well downhill.

cards.front: What is an ion's equilibrium potential?
cards.back: The one membrane voltage at which the concentration and voltage terms cancel, so the ion has no net push in or out. Setting ΔG = 0 and solving for voltage gives the Nernst equation.
cards.quote: For each ion there is one voltage where the two parts cancel exactly, so the ion has no net push in or out.

cards.front: K⁺ is 4 mM outside and 140 mM inside at 37 °C, where RT/F ≈ 26.7 mV. Calculate E_K.
A cell has K⁺ at 4 mM outside and 140 mM inside, so E_K is about −95 mV. K⁺ channels open while the membrane is held first at −80 mV, then at −110 mV. Which way does K⁺ flow in each case?
cards.back: At −80 mV, outward: the concentration term outweighs the voltage term. At −110 mV, inward: the voltage is more negative than E_K, so the voltage term outweighs the concentration term.
cards.why: K⁺ has no net push only at E_K; on either side of it, the larger term wins.
cards.quote: A negative inside pulls positive ions in and pushes negative ions out.

cards.front: Why does a cell's resting membrane potential sit near E_K rather than near E_Na?
cards.back: At rest the membrane is most permeable to K⁺, so the resting potential sits near K⁺'s equilibrium potential.
cards.quote: At rest the membrane is most permeable to K⁺, so the resting potential sits near K⁺'s equilibrium potential.

cards.front: How does a channel differ from a carrier in mechanism and speed?
cards.back: A channel is a pore, open to both sides at once when gated open; it is fast, typically millions of ions per second. A carrier uses alternating access, never open to both sides at once, and is slower.
cards.why: The fastest potassium channels reach about 10⁸ ions per second.
cards.quote: It is never open to both sides at once, and it is slower than a channel.
cards.section: Moving things across: channels, carriers and paying for uphill

cards.front: Classify each on the two transport axes (mechanism; energy): an aquaporin, the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase, and SGLT1.
cards.back: Aquaporin: channel, downhill. Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase: carrier, uphill, spends ATP (a pump). SGLT1: carrier, uphill, spends sodium's downhill run (a coupled transporter).
cards.why: A pore open to both sides can only let solutes run downhill, so no channel moves anything uphill.
cards.quote: Transport proteins differ on two separate axes, one for each question.
cards.section: Moving things across: channels, carriers and paying for uphill

cards.front: What does the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase move per ATP, and what makes it a P-type ATPase?
cards.back: It ejects 3 Na⁺ and imports 2 K⁺ per ATP. It phosphorylates one of its own aspartate residues, and that phosphoaspartate intermediate drives its shape change.
cards.quote: ejects 3 sodium ions and imports 2 potassium ions per ATP
cards.section: The pump that charges the battery

cards.front: Moving 1 mol Na⁺ out of a cell costs about +13.2 kJ, and moving 1 mol K⁺ in costs about +2.4 kJ. Can one ATP (roughly 50 to 57 kJ/mol under cell conditions) pay for one Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase cycle?
cards.back: Cost = 3 × 13.2 + 2 × 2.4 = 39.6 + 4.8 ≈ 44 kJ/mol. Yes: the cycle fits inside one ATP with a modest margin.
cards.quote: The pump fits inside one ATP, with a modest margin.
cards.section: The pump that charges the battery

cards.front: What is secondary active transport, and how do a symporter and an antiporter differ?
cards.back: A solute running downhill drags another uphill, with no ATP spent at that step. Symporters move both the same way (SGLT1: Na⁺ and glucose in); antiporters move them opposite ways (Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger: Na⁺ in, Ca²⁺ out).
cards.quote: Couple a solute running downhill to another being dragged uphill, and you get uphill transport with no ATP spent at that step.

cards.front: SGLT1 couples 2 Na⁺ to each glucose; each Na⁺ entering releases about 13.2 kJ/mol (RT = 2.58 kJ/mol). What is the largest glucose ratio (inside : outside) it can hold, and what would 1 Na⁺ per glucose allow?
cards.why: Glucose is uncharged, so only its concentration term counts.
cards.quote: One sodium per glucose would allow only about 170-fold.

cards.front: Suppose a cell's membrane potential collapses to 0 mV while Na⁺ stays at 145 mM outside and 12 mM inside. Estimate the largest glucose gradient SGLT1 (2 Na⁺ per glucose) could now hold.
cards.back: With no voltage term, each Na⁺ releases only 2.58 × ln(145/12) ≈ 6.4 kJ/mol; two give ≈ 12.9 kJ/mol. Then e^(12.9/2.58) = (145/12)² ≈ 150-fold, far below the ~28,000-fold at −70 mV.
cards.why: Rests on ΔG = concentration term + voltage term for Na⁺, and on glucose being uncharged.
cards.quote: Glucose is uncharged, so only its concentration term counts

cards.front: Digitalis inhibits the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase in heart muscle cells. Trace the effect on intracellular Ca²⁺ and on contraction, and say why the dose is risky.
cards.back: Na⁺ backs up inside, the Na⁺ gradient shrinks, the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger slows, Ca²⁺ accumulates, and each beat hits harder. Too much causes calcium-overload arrhythmias.
cards.why: Links the pump that builds the Na⁺ gradient to the antiporter that spends it.
cards.quote: the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger slows because the sodium gradient it spends has shrunk, calcium accumulates, and each heartbeat hits harder

cards.front: Gliflozins block SGLT2, the kidney's sodium-glucose symporter that normally reclaims filtered glucose. Predict the effect on urine and blood glucose.
cards.back: Glucose spills into the urine and blood sugar falls, because filtered glucose is no longer pulled back uphill on sodium's gradient.
cards.quote: so glucose spills into the urine and blood sugar falls

cards.front: A K⁺ channel passes K⁺ over 1,000 times more readily than the smaller Na⁺. In the snug-fit picture, how does the selectivity filter reject Na⁺?
cards.back: It works on the toll, not size. The eight oxygens of a site replace K⁺'s water closely, repaying its desolvation cost. Na⁺ is too small to touch all eight at once, is not repaid, and stalls.
cards.quote: The filter repays nearly all of K⁺'s toll and falls short on Na⁺'s.
cards.section: Lowering the toll exactly: the potassium channel filter

cards.front: A 1000-to-1 K⁺ preference at 37 °C (RT = 2.58 kJ/mol) needs what free-energy difference? Given that Na⁺'s hydration energy exceeds K⁺'s by about 70 kJ/mol, how much more energy could the filter give back to Na⁺ than to K⁺ and still select K⁺?
cards.back: RT × ln(1000) = 2.58 × 6.91 ≈ 17.8 kJ/mol. The filter could give Na⁺ up to about 70 − 18 ≈ 52 kJ/mol more and still pass K⁺ a thousand times better.
cards.why: Selectivity is the shortfall in repaying Na⁺'s extra toll; small differences in a huge toll are enough.
cards.quote: It can even give Na⁺ more energy back than K⁺, as much as about 52 kJ/mol more
cards.section: Lowering the toll exactly: the potassium channel filter

cards.front: If the K⁺ channel filter binds K⁺ tightly enough to be selective, why does K⁺ leave fast (the knock-on mechanism)?
cards.back: Probably crowding: several K⁺ ions sit in the filter at once, and like charges repel. When a second ion enters, the repulsion lowers the barrier for the leading ion to leave.
cards.quote: When a second ion enters, the repulsion between the ions lowers the barrier for the leading ion to leave.
cards.section: Lowering the toll exactly: the potassium channel filter

cards.front: CFTR belongs to a family that is mostly ATP-powered pumps, and it uses ATP. Why is it a channel and not a pump?
cards.back: Once PKA phosphorylates its regulatory domain, ATP binding gates the pore open, and chloride flows down its own electrochemical gradient. ATP opens the gate; it does not pay for the move.
cards.quote: ATP opens the gate. It does not pay for the move.
cards.section: CFTR: a channel built from a pump family

cards.front: A patient with ΔF508 CFTR is given only a potentiator, a drug that helps channels already at the cell surface open. Predict the benefit, and why.
cards.back: Little. ΔF508 CFTR misfolds and is mostly destroyed in the endoplasmic reticulum, so few channels reach the surface. A corrector, which helps folding and delivery, is needed too.
cards.quote: a potentiator alone has little to work on, because most of the channel never arrives
cards.section: CFTR: a channel built from a pump family

cards.front: A drug with a carboxylate group (pKa 4) must reach a target inside the cell but crosses membranes poorly. Predict the effect of masking the carboxylate as an ester.
cards.back: It should cross far faster. At pH 7 only about 1 in 1,000 molecules is uncharged; the charged form pays the toll for leaving water. The uncharged ester does not, and cellular esterases can restore the active acid inside.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that charge sets the desolvation toll, as with tryptophan versus indole.
cards.quote: At pH 7, three units above the pKa, only about one molecule in a thousand is uncharged.

cards.front: A uniporter in the membrane happens to carry a negatively charged drug. With equal drug concentrations to start and a negative-inside membrane, where does the drug end up, and how could it be pulled in?
cards.back: Less concentrated inside than outside: a uniporter only moves the drug down its electrochemical gradient, and the negative inside pushes anions out. A carrier coupled to Na⁺ could pull it in uphill, as SGLT1 does glucose.
cards.why: Speed and direction are separate questions; the transporter fixes speed, the gradient sets direction.
cards.quote: the negative inside pushes an anion out, so a uniporter alone would leave the drug less concentrated inside than outside

cards.front: Tetrodotoxin (pufferfish) and saxitoxin (paralytic shellfish poisoning) both cause paralysis. Where do they act, and why does that paralyze?
cards.back: They plug the outer mouth of voltage-gated sodium channels. Na⁺ cannot enter, so nerves cannot depolarize and action potentials cannot fire.
cards.quote: both plug the outer mouth of voltage-gated sodium channels, so nerves cannot depolarize and the victim is paralyzed

cards.front: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates Ser530 in the COX-1 substrate channel; ibuprofen binds the same site reversibly. Predict the effect of taking ibuprofen just before low-dose aspirin.
cards.back: Ibuprofen can shield the site and blunt aspirin's lasting antiplatelet effect. Normally aspirin's block lasts a platelet's whole life, because platelets have no nucleus and cannot make new COX-1.
cards.why: How much heart protection is lost is still unclear.
cards.quote: Ibuprofen competes for the same site reversibly, so taking ibuprofen before aspirin can shield the site and blunt aspirin's antiplatelet effect

cards.front: Vasopressin normally inserts aquaporin-2 into the kidney collecting-duct membrane. Predict what happens when that regulation fails.
cards.back: The kidneys cannot concentrate urine, and a person can pass up to about 20 liters of dilute urine a day: diabetes insipidus.
cards.quote: when that regulation fails, the kidneys cannot concentrate urine and a person can pass up to about 20 liters of dilute urine a day
cards.section: How an aquaporin passes water but not protons
